extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Plato / classical literature and philosophy; literary critics and teachers studying the Republic
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading and critical analysis of Plato's Republic focusing on its dramatic structure, argumentative methods, recurring figures/allegories, and the philosophical positions presented by interlocutors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of recurring figures and allegory
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures such as the cave (Book VII), the composite animal (Book IX), the noble captain/ship/true pilot (Book VI), the dog, the marriage of the portionless maiden, or the drones and wasps serve as recapitulations or allegories linking parts of the work and recalling previous discussions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and interpret recurring images as structural links and mnemonic recapitulations; see them as allegorical devices that recall earlier divisions of knowledge or parts of the soul. Anti-pattern: treating these figures as isolated ornaments rather than as connective motifs that unify long passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faithfulness to Socratic characterisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato is 'most true to the character of his master' when he depicts Socrates as 'not of this world' — an 'unwearied and disinterested seeker after truth' who shows moderation toward those in error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing passages, check whether portrayals preserve Socratic traits: disinterest, persistent questioning, pity rather than wrath toward the many. Beware attributing all paradoxes in the Republic directly to the historical Socrates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening scene and dramatic framing
rubrics_metrics.description: The Dialogue opens with a vivid Greek scene (a festival at the Piraeus) and is presented as Socrates' recital to a small party; the rhetorical advantage of reciting the Dialogue is used and the audience is not repeatedly invoked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how scene-setting, the selection of interlocutors, and the rhetorical frame (recital after a festival) shape the philosophical inquiry. Note the restraint in distracting references to the audience — the dramatic frame focuses attention on the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction of philosophical problems via concrete portraits
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato prepares for the long discourse (e.g., on justice) by a portrait of the just man (Cephalus' description of old age) which serves as a natural frontispiece to the inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for how Plato begins with particular, familiar portraits or anecdotes to motivate abstract inquiry. Anti-pattern: expecting immediate abstract definitions without preliminary illustrative material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialectical method and interrogation
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'interrogation' of moral ideas — questioning established definitions (Simonides, poets), using casuistry, counterexamples, and the dialectical enlargement of concepts — is central to the argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace Socratic questioning, identify when definitions are probed by counterexamples or casuistic exceptions, and follow the progressive enlargement of concepts. Note that dialectic often proceeds indirectly and expands the application of ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing definitions by counterexamples and casuistry
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple definitions (e.g., 'to tell the truth and pay your debts', or 'do good to friends and harm to enemies') are tested against particular cases (returning a sword to a mad friend) and shown to be inadequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate proposed definitions by constructing plausible counterexamples. Recognize casuistry as a legitimate and ancient tool for exposing conflicts between general precepts and particular circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of reductio and analogies (notably the arts analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato frequently uses reductio ad absurdum and analogies (e.g., comparing justice to the arts: no external interest; not aiming at excess) to reveal contradictions and to clarify the nature of virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an analogy is used, test its scope and limits: analogies can illuminate but also mislead. Expect reductio to expose absurd consequences (e.g., 'justice is a thief') and thereby push the argument forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of popular authorities (poets, common sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: The authority of poets and common opinion is often set aside; poets are appealed to and then critiqued, and popular moralities (the temporal rewards of justice) are examined and rejected as the final ground of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how Plato uses and then dismantles popular and poetic authorities — look for passages where poets are implicated in false pictures of rewards and punishments. Beware taking popular epitomes as philosophically decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic presentation of opposing theses
rubrics_metrics.description: Opposing views are given life through interlocutors (Thrasymachus, Glaucon, Adeimantus), often represented rhetorically (e.g., Thrasymachus' roar), and their positions (might is right; injustice more profitable) are tested in debate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse not only the content of opposing theses but also their rhetorical embodiment; examine how character and rhetoric affect the force and reception of the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing an ideal State to ground individual justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato often proceeds from the State to the individual: he restores man to his natural condition and frames an ideal State as the starting point for defining justice, before applying the results to the soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting the Republic, follow the methodological move from polis to person: evaluate the perfect State as a device to reveal the internal nature of justice in the individual. Do not expect an immediate, purely individualistic account of justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of thought-experiments and role-reversal tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought-experiments (e.g., the Ring of Gyges) and hypothetical role reversals (just thought unjust, unjust thought just) are employed to test whether justice is intrinsic or merely instrumental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight and examine such thought-experiments as methodological probes that isolate the internal value of justice. Consider how excluding reputation or external rewards tightens the test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of goods and the link between justice and happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Goods are classified (desirable in themselves; desirable for themselves and results; desirable for results only), and justice is placed among goods desirable both in themselves and for their results; justice is linked to happiness as the soul's excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace Plato's taxonomy of goods and how it safeguards the internal value of justice; evaluate arguments that identify justice with the virtue that realizes the soul's end (happiness). Note the author's caution about modern confusions over 'happiness.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention to linguistic accuracy and conceptual limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The commentary flags imprecise or novel language (e.g., 'art of pay') and flawed locutions ('men who are injured are made more unjust'), urging careful attention to phrases that may extend concepts beyond their ordinary use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to linguistic slips or neologisms that affect the argument; distinguish between persuasive rhetorical turns and genuine conceptual innovations. Corrective reading can reveal where Plato's analogies overextend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical notion of measure and harmony
rubrics_metrics.description: A Hellenic sentiment sees the good as finite, governed by measure, equality, order, unity, proportion; virtue is conceived as harmony (soul with body; parts of soul with one another) rather than merely maximal excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret Platonic ethics in terms of proportion and harmony; look for imagery of musical harmony and limits. Avoid reading Plato solely through later teleological or utilitarian categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirectness and progressive development of answers
rubrics_metrics.description: Socrates often answers indirectly: he enlarges the problem, sets up idealized situations, and only after an extended dialectic intimates the reconciliation of justice and happiness; nothing is concluded hastily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the argumentative trajectory rather than demand immediate definitions. Expect provisional positions and staged developments; evaluate the movement of thought across books rather than isolated passages.
